content:
Mathlib has moved to the module system a while ago, but still does not utilize many of its features widely.

In particular, about 94% of import lines in mathlib (more or less 25k/27k) are still public import's. A large number of those could be private however. I sampled 300 random public import's and 98 of them could be private (though this includes imports that could be removed outright).
Since we don't have too many private defs and theorems, an import can usually be private whenever it is only used in proofs.

Privatizing imports en masse could potentially help perfomance, i.e. due to instance synthesis and tactics have less to look up, and (if I understand correctly from #mathlib4 > Mathlib has moved to the new module system ) help rebuilding faster. Additionally, this is supported by the view that a file should only import what it really needs.

However, private imports aren't transitive, so privatizing imports requires a lot of imports to be added to downstream files, so the total lines of imports would likely increase quite a bit. Additionally, privatizing whenever possible might cause very leaf-y files (i.e. probability theory) to still have to import some very core files, which might be slightly annoying.

It is also not a trivial task at all to privatize imports; today I tried to privatize importing of ~30 files in MeasureTheory which contain no defs etc. (so should be relatively unroblematic at least in theory), but even that caused huge headaches and I gave up before even coming close to finishing.

So I am wondering about the following:

1) Is it beneficial / worth it to privatize many public imports?

2) If yes, what would be an efficient way? Certainly one would need some kind of automation, but as I aid before, this is not a trivial task. Certainly it would be better to privatize in small chunks (among other reasons to be able to prevent unexpected perfomance changes).
First doing files close to the core causes much more downstream failures, but requires less iterations then starting from leaf files.

3) Mathlib still contains many (>20%) imports which are outright redundant; i.e. can be removed from a file. In #PR reviews > #41222 remove many redundant imports @Yaël Dillies said it would be preferable to first privatize imports and only then reduce imports en masse, as this would require less restoring of imports.
On the other hand, first privatizing would (temporarily) redundantly privatize many imports that could just be removed outright and any large scale privatization would need to add many imports one way or the other.
So (again, if yes to 1)) would first privatizing and then reducing or first reducing and then privatizing be a better approach?

Privatizing imports en masse could potentially help perfomance, i.e. due to instance synthesis and tactics have less to look up, and (if I understand correctly from mathlib4 > Mathlib has moved to the new module system ) help rebuilding faster.

The main concern to me is breaking user projects downstream.

I am still not convinced on the performance gains. That is a testable claim so you should run the experiment.

Re: redundant imports, PR #41222 achieved:

> ✅ build//instructions: **-85.8G** (**-0.06%**)

which is not enough to justify a 4000 line diff.

I'm not sure that benchmarking the entire project gives the whole picture; IIUC the point of private imports in the module system is to avoid rebuilds when private data of privately imported modules changes. This could still be a massive QoL win for people working in Mathlib even if radar reports +0.0%.

I agree, privatization could be good QoL and general tech debt / hygiene practices. And since Yaël suggested it, I'm inclined to think we should do it. Felix pls ping me if you make a PR I'd love to see what happens.

My understanding is that the community is working on an automated solution for this already via shake. See e.g. this thread #mathlib4 > shake @ 💬 . You might want to take up the conversation there if shake still isn't doing everything you want here.

Felix Pernegger said:

today I tried to privatize importing of ~30 files in MeasureTheory which contain no defs etc. (so should be relatively unroblematic at least in theory), but even that caused huge headaches and I gave up before even coming close to finishing.

I strongly advise not spending your precious human time on such a menial task, and instead get an LLM to do it for you

Yaël Dillies said:

I strongly advise not spending your precious human time on such a menial task, and instead get an LLM to do it for you

I did this of course, but the LLM couldnt easily solve it as well :)

Jack McCarthy said:

The main concern to me is breaking user projects downstream.

This only occurs when the downstream projects also use modules. In this case they should be able to figure out public/private import changes.

Felix's test PR about this (#42045) got sent to me to review (since it happened to involve a number theory file) but I really don't feel I am the right person to judge whether it's a good idea or not.

IMHO, if mathlib is to make this change, it should be done consistently across all of mathlib in one go, and based on consistent general criteria discussed and agreed by the community as a whole, not just piecemeal experimentation on individual files.

A wholesale automated minimization would also work best for judging the impact (and potentially adaptation) of downstream projects I would say. I've been having similar thoughts on if and how we could minimize core analogously, though no concrete plans there at this point
